title: What is Biosafety?
description: Policies, protocols, and practices to minimize exposure to harmful biological agents and protect people and the environment.

content.text: Biosafety is shaped by scientific progress and emerging risks. The scientific breakthroughs of Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch in the 1890s revealed the dangers of biological hazards, laying the foundation for biosafety.

The increasing number of laboratory-acquired infections (LAIs) in the mid-20th century emphasized the need for stricter laboratory safety protocols. The 1970s marked a turning point when biosafety emerged as a distinct discipline, spurred by international classification systems and pivotal discussions.

From the 1980s onward, global conventions and standards were established to regulate biological research and laboratory safety. The scope of biosafety expanded in the 1990s, moving beyond laboratories to address risks in agriculture, environmental protection, and food safety. In 2020, the WHO updated its Laboratory Biosafety Manual to cover all "biological agents," not just pathogens and toxins.
Biosafety Cabinets (BSCs)
Biosafety cabinets are essential for handling hazardous biological materials. They are classified into three main types:

items: Class I BSCs: protect the user and the environment but do not safeguard samples.
Class II BSCs: most common; provide personnel, product, and environmental protection (types A2, B1, and B2).
Class III BSCs: maximum containment; fully enclosed, gas-tight systems for high-risk pathogens such as Ebola and smallpox.

content.text: Proper PPE—including gloves, lab coats, face shields, and respirators—acts as a critical barrier against exposure. The choice of PPE depends on the biosafety level (BSL) of the work being conducted.
Autoclaving is the gold standard for deactivating biohazardous waste. For surface decontamination, chemical disinfectants such as bleach and hydrogen peroxide vapor are used.

title: Understanding Biosafety Levels (BSL): The Cornerstone of Effective Risk Assessment
description: How BSL-1 to BSL-4 and dynamic risk assessment combine to select controls and keep labs and communities safe.

content.text: In the world of biological research and clinical diagnostics, safety is not a matter of chance—it is a matter of choice. This framework protects personnel, the environment, and the community from accidental exposure to infectious agents. At its heart: Biosafety Levels (BSL) and Risk Assessment.
BSL-1 through BSL-4 are tiers of biocontainment defined by practices, safety equipment, and facility design.

items: Laboratory Practices and Techniques: SOPs for safe handling.
Safety Equipment: Primary barriers such as BSCs and PPE.
Facility Design and Construction: Ventilation, airlocks, waste treatment.
BSL-1: Non-pathogenic agents; standard microbiology practices.
BSL-2: Moderate-risk agents (e.g., S. aureus, HBV); enhanced PPE, signage, Class I/II BSCs.
BSL-3: Serious or lethal respiratory agents (e.g., M. tuberculosis, SARS-CoV-2); negative pressure, restricted access, non-recirculated exhaust.
BSL-4: High-risk, no treatment/vaccine (e.g., Ebola, Marburg); maximum containment, positive-pressure suits.

content.text: Selecting the appropriate BSL results from a dynamic risk assessment of agent hazards, procedures, personnel, and facility capabilities.

items: Agent Hazards: Pathogenicity, infectious dose, treatment/vaccines.
Personnel Competence: Training, proficiency, immunological status.

sections.title: How BSL and Risk Assessment Work Together

content.text: BSL defines baseline controls; risk assessment decides the level and additional precautions for specific procedures (e.g., aerosol-generating work may require escalation).
A safe lab integrates prescribed BSL controls with continuous risk assessment. Re-evaluate risks with every new experiment, agent, or procedure change.

sections.title: What is Cell Culture? A Beginner's Guide
sections.description: Learn the fundamentals of cell culture: how scientists grow and study living cells in a laboratory setting, from primary cells to immortalized cell lines.

content.text: Cell culture is one of the most important techniques in modern biology. Whether it is for studying cancer, making vaccines, testing drugs, or growing stem cells for therapy, many scientific discoveries begin with one simple activity—growing cells outside of the body. In essence, cell culture allows scientists to nurture and study living cells in a carefully controlled environment, making it possible to explore how cells function, respond, and adapt to different conditions.

At its core, cell culture is the process of growing cells in a laboratory setting rather than in their natural environment. Instead of residing inside an organism, the cells are placed in a flask or dish and supplied with the nutrients, temperature, and atmosphere they need to survive and multiply. You can think of this as giving cells a miniature home—one where researchers can safely observe and experiment on them under highly regulated conditions.

Scientists culture cells for many reasons. It allows them to study how cells grow, divide, and communicate without the complexity of working inside an entire organism. Through cell culture, researchers can examine how cells respond to drugs, toxins, or environmental stress. They can investigate which genes turn on or off during disease and even engineer cells to produce useful compounds such as hormones, antibodies, and vaccines. Because cells can be kept alive for weeks or even years, experiments can be repeated under consistent conditions, leading to more reliable data.

sections.title: Types of Cells Used in Culture

content.text: There are two main kinds of cells used in culture. Primary cells are taken directly from living tissues such as skin, blood, or organs. They behave very similarly to how they would inside the body, which makes them valuable for studying real biological processes. However, primary cells are fragile, have a limited lifespan, and require delicate handling. The second type, known as cell lines, are cells that have adapted to grow continuously and divide indefinitely. They are easier to maintain and are widely used in research and industry. Famous examples include HeLa cells, derived from cervical cancer, and CHO cells, which are commonly used to produce therapeutic proteins.

Cells cannot survive on their own; they need a carefully controlled environment. In a cell culture laboratory, everything must be kept sterile to prevent contamination by bacteria, fungi, or yeast. Scientists work inside a biosafety cabinet that provides a clean, filtered workspace. The cells are fed with a nutrient-rich liquid known as the culture medium, which contains sugars, amino acids, salts, vitamins, and growth factors that mimic the natural fluids surrounding cells in the body. Some media formulations also contain serum, which provides additional hormones and proteins needed for cell growth.

The physical conditions are equally important. Most mammalian cells require a temperature of around 37°C, the same as the human body, and a carbon dioxide level of about five percent to keep the medium at the correct pH. These conditions are maintained inside a specialized incubator. Cells are usually grown in sterile plastic vessels such as flasks, plates, or dishes that are specially treated to help them attach to the surface and spread out.

A typical cell culture session follows a simple rhythm. The process often begins by thawing frozen cells or isolating a fresh sample. The cells are transferred into a flask containing warm medium and placed in the incubator to allow them to attach and begin dividing. Researchers regularly observe them under a microscope to check their health and replace the medium every few days to replenish nutrients. When the cells become crowded, they are subcultured, meaning a portion is transferred into a new vessel with fresh medium. If the culture is no longer needed, it can be frozen for long-term storage in liquid nitrogen. This cycle of growth, maintenance, and monitoring forms the foundation of every cell culture experiment.

Despite its routine nature, cell culture comes with challenges. Contamination is one of the most common problems, often recognized by cloudy media or an unusual odor. Overgrown cultures can also suffer from stress, changing their shape and behavior. Even experienced scientists must troubleshoot issues related to slow growth or unexpected results, which makes patience and precision key traits in this field.

Cell culture has countless applications. In biomedical research, it allows scientists to study disease mechanisms, test new drugs, and explore genetic functions. In biotechnology, cultured cells are used to produce vaccines, enzymes, and therapeutic antibodies. In regenerative medicine, they serve as the foundation for developing tissues and organs that can one day repair or replace damaged parts of the human body. Even in education, cell culture is an essential teaching tool that helps students understand how cells behave and interact with their environment.

Ultimately, cell culture has transformed the landscape of biological and medical research. By providing a way to observe cells directly, it has paved the way for breakthroughs in cancer treatment, vaccine development, and biotechnology. For beginners, learning cell culture opens the door to a wide range of scientific and industrial careers. It remains a cornerstone skill of modern life sciences—one that continues to shape the future of medicine and discovery.
